title: Cost, Speed and Quality - One Law Firm's Quest to Deliver All Three (Laurence Brown, Partner EIP and Head of Visser AI)
author: Laurence Brown

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Brown identifies client budget pressure and demand for effective AI use, while describing EIP as still transitioning from traditional practice. He does not address whether automation is removing junior training work, creating a verification-expertise paradox, or requiring reconstructed apprenticeship.
qs: But what we've realized is that clients are demanding that their lawyers use AI effectively.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Brown accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI should augment rather than remove lawyers and materially extends it with a concrete patent-practice model: AI-assisted workflows paired with lower, value-oriented fixed fees. His account illustrates how efficiency gains can be shared with clients while preserving attorney-led delivery, although the reported savings are practice-based rather than independently validated.
qs: It's a shift on the client side from the classic billable hour-based pricing, basically to fixed fees, where you're agreeing a cost based on the value that the client sees in the work.
I think you can match the value the client wants with the price they are prepared to pay and deliver that with the attorneys not being cut out.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Brown supports the cluster’s core proposition that meaningful AI adoption requires redesigned working methods rather than isolated chatbot use, and links this transition to client budget pressure and demand for demonstrable benefits. His discussion of deregulation also aligns with the cluster’s view that alternative ownership and multidisciplinary structures can widen organisational options, though the excerpts offer little evidence on apprenticeship, verification or realised pricing outcomes.
qs: To go AI-native, you need to take that next step up to really leveraging the AI, knowing how you can change the way you work to benefit from that.
But what we've realized is that clients are demanding that their lawyers use AI effectively.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition by presenting legal AI as a specialised hybrid practice model rather than a standalone subscription, with patent-specific AI accelerating drafting while preserving time for human insight. Its reported 30% cost reduction also supports the claimed economic potential, although the absence of a baseline or measured quality assessment leaves verification and defensibility unresolved.
qs: They built an entirely new model of legal practice.
By leveraging cutting-edge specific patent AI, the firm started delivering patent drafts faster with more time for human insight.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by advocating AI adoption while framing non-use as a possible future malpractice issue, not an existing professional duty. Its claims about benefits and data safety are personal assurances rather than demonstrated legal or security evidence.
qs: At some point, does it become malpractice not to use AI?

I think it does, because already I'm seeing that I'm just, across all my work, all my clients, I'm trying to do my best to persuade them of the benefits of AI and that it's safe, their data is safe, and it's a brave new world.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Brown supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI’s value depends on redesigning workflows rather than merely adding a chat assistant to existing tools. He also recognises genuine confidentiality and governance risks requiring safeguards, while cautioning that overly risk-centred regulation can impede beneficial adoption. He does not materially address the cluster’s broader evidence on jagged capability, verification burdens or labour effects.
qs: But you get so much more from thinking away from that, thinking, okay, now we've got AI, how can we change it?

Actually, the most genuine thing of it is the real recognition that LLMs are different from any other cloud-based resource, in that if you haven't agreed full all the confidentiality requirements, no data retention, no use for training, you do run the risk of your invention, which you have to keep confidential.

kp.k: AI-native practice requires redesigned work, not merely prompting
kp.d: Brown defines AI-native broadly enough to include both minimally human firms and firms employing attorneys trained to work differently with AI. His defining condition is changing how work is performed to exploit AI, rather than simply using ChatGPT effectively.
qs: AI-native law firm is an inclusive term that includes fully AI-powered law firms, where the human involvement is minimal, and then ones which include human attorneys.
But the human attorneys in an AI-native firm are ones who expect to be working with AI, who know how to use it, who are trained in different ways of working.
To go AI-native, you need to take that next step up to really leveraging the AI, knowing how you can change the way you work to benefit from that.

kp.k: Visser AI is a legal service within EIP
kp.d: Correcting the host's suggestion that Visser is a software company, Brown describes it as EIP's AI-native service or department, using and evaluating external tools. EIP still provides traditional services and remains in transition. Brown anticipates an increasing AI-native share of work, potentially reaching all work surprisingly quickly, but gives no timetable.
qs: So Visser AI is a service offered by EIP.
EIP still exists as a law firm in the traditional sense. We still do work for clients in the traditional ways.
I suppose it's almost like a department, it's the AI-native part of EIP.
I can just see based on take up so far, there's going to be an increasing proportion of work until maybe surprisingly fast that it's just all work, is AI-Native.

kp.k: Client budget pressure encourages collaborative fixed-fee pricing
kp.d: Brown reports clients demanding demonstrable AI efficiencies rather than superficial adoption. He distinguishes reports of unilateral budget cuts from his own clients' more collaborative negotiations over lower fixed fees reflecting perceived value. He does not report clients insisting that billing mechanically track every AI-enabled reduction in task time.
qs: they're coming under pressure to cut their budgets and to not just have the lawyers typing into ChatGPT and their internal metrics are asking them to see the benefits of it.
I have to admit that's not how my clients have approached it.
It tends to be more of a collaborative conversation of, look, we can use AI, we can make a saving in terms of the time, let's agree a budget that's reasonable.
It's a shift on the client side from the classic billable hour-based pricing, basically to fixed fees, where you're agreeing a cost based on the value that the client sees in the work.

kp.k: Brown claims hybrid intelligence breaks the cost-quality-speed tradeoff
kp.d: Brown argues that redesigned AI-assisted work can simultaneously deliver faster turnaround, high quality and lower cost. He illustrates the value with an urgent patent filing before disclosure. This is a practitioner claim rather than a reported comparative outcome study, and he stresses that EIP's quality-focused clients will not accept quality reductions.
qs: Now, a client can benefit from quick turnarounds, high quality and lower cost, but there is a value in that.
That patent application is far ahead now with AI assistance than it would have been without.
That conversation is predicated on the quality can't drop.

kp.k: Fixed fees retain cost discipline and reward filing scale
kp.d: Brown says pricing still incorporates attorney time, salaries and overhead, with historical billing analysis informing offers to existing clients. He identifies volume filers as especially well positioned to benefit from client familiarity and economies of scale, illustrating this with 100 cases. He reports 30 percent as a standard client cost reduction, without supplying an audited sample or measurement period, and contrasts mutually beneficial fixed fees with caps that leave firms bearing overruns.
qs: Fundamentally, you have still got to look at how long it takes.
Those firms that will most benefit from AI are volume filers because there are real economies of scale.
When you're then working on 100 cases, they get huge benefits.
You bill under the cap, you bill for the time, but if you go over the cap, then you can't recover that cost.
Clients see a meaningful cost reduction. We talk about 30 percent as a standard one.

kp.k: Parallel workflows redistribute senior and junior attorney tasks
kp.d: Brown describes moving beyond linear patent production while retaining EIP's two-attorney quality approach. Senior attorneys can work on claims while junior attorneys use the same source materials to structure drafts and prepare supporting material. This describes changed task coordination, not a reported reduction in junior headcount or associate-to-partner leverage.
qs: We've always had the key selling point of EIP is two pairs of attorney eyes on every piece of work.
We can redesign the workflows to keep that quality benefit, but also there's more scope for working in parallel.
In a patent draft, for example, a senior attorney can be working on the claims at the same time as the more junior attorney is structuring the draft, doing the prep work ahead of the claims.

kp.k: AI assists invention analysis but struggles with claim language
kp.d: Brown reports using AI before inventor meetings to probe inventions and identify additional questions, and afterward to extract technical details from transcripts. He regards claim drafting as a continuing weakness requiring human linguistic understanding, despite AI's usefulness in locating relevant inventor statements. These are observations from his practice rather than quantified task-performance results.
qs: As an attorney, you've already had a chance to test the invention, probe it using AI.
I find basically always it comes up with useful extra questions to gather more information.
From the transcript, you're using AI to pull out key details in a way that is really hard.
it doesn't have the understanding of language to write a really good patent claim.
That's where human understanding comes in.

kp.k: Human verification remains central alongside additional AI critiques
kp.d: Brown claims AI can improve the readability of patent drafts, but describes humans identifying inaccuracies and fully checking the work. EIP also requests critiques from a fresh AI instance, sometimes using a different model and providing both the draft and source information. AI critique supplements rather than replaces human verification.
qs: One of the best things of AI drafting, it can do a better job at making something that's readable than a human can.
Then the human comes in and spots those bits where it's not quite right.
Everything is fully checked and we get the AI to check as well.
We spin up a new instance, sometimes even a different model, feed it the draft and all the information, get it to critique it in addition to our own human review.

kp.k: Internal tool comparisons found substantial patent-drafting quality differences
kp.d: Brown describes an internal comparison conducted probably 18 months before the interview, giving six leading patent-AI providers identical information for drafting a patent specification and asking other EIP partners to rate and rank outputs. He reports large quality differences, but provides no scores or fuller testing protocol. Visser uses Patently; Brown says ongoing comparisons favor it over EIP's general-purpose Microsoft Copilot for specialist work, while Copilot performs proofreading and summarization well.
qs: I did a big test probably 18 months ago now, comparing the six leading Patent AI providers at that point, and I made it as scientific as I could.
they basically all got given the same information to draft a patent specification.
Then I asked others of the partners at EIP to rate them and rank them in terms of which was best.
some of them were awful, and others are surprisingly good.
I find proofreading, summarizing tasks can be excellently done by, we use Microsoft Copilot at EIP as our general purpose.

kp.k: Specialist tools add context management and workflow support
kp.d: Brown attributes Patently's usefulness to patent-specific setup, easier context switching and reuse, and an interface supporting different workflows, while explicitly disclaiming expertise in its underlying implementation. He argues that simply adding a specialist chatbot to Word captures less benefit than reconsidering the production process.
qs: So Patently itself is built on top of the various models and their APIs that are available.
I'm not an expert in what they've done behind the scenes
you can effectively ask it patent questions without needing to phrase it in such a careful way as you do with Co-Pilot.
And you can spin up new AIs, reusing context, using new context.
They're designed to help you work efficiently as well as having the powered AI behind it.

kp.k: AI dialogue may improve attorneys' experience of chargeable work
kp.d: Brown reports finding AI-assisted work more enjoyable and attributes this tentatively to its conversational character. He explicitly allows that novelty may explain the effect. His account retains the challenge of recording eight, nine or ten chargeable hours in a long day rather than claiming reduced working hours.
qs: One is from an attorney point of view, it's actually quite fun working with AI.
Now, I don't know if that's just novelty or change, but something about it changes the way that you're working.
That's recording eight, nine, ten in a really long day, chargeable hours is still a real mental challenge, but the difference is it feels a lot more fun.
I think it's the dialogue aspects.

kp.k: Confidentiality safeguards are essential, but compliance can discourage adoption
kp.d: Brown regards confidentiality, no data retention and no training on client material as vital for patent work, and says EIP's Copilot deployment is configured accordingly. He criticizes European patent-profession guidance for reinforcing risk aversion, while acknowledging legitimate leakage and billing concerns. His example of a firm requiring a form for every AI use is explicitly secondhand; he identifies no particular binding rule.
qs: It's all fully set up to be confidential. No data retention, no training, vital for patent work to keep it all confidential.
if you haven't agreed full all the confidentiality requirements, no data retention, no use for training, you do run the risk of your invention, which you have to keep confidential.
I heard of another firm that in order to meet that regulation, it asks all their attorneys to fill in a form every time they use AI.
I think that's the challenge of the regulation, was it was phrasing it from a risk-based point of view, and it played to a conservative industry that's like, yes, this is risky.

kp.k: Nonuse of AI is framed as a future professional concern
kp.d: Brown proposes reversing the ethical discussion to ask whether withholding AI's benefits disserves clients. Host Chad Main raises the stronger possibility that not using AI, even to challenge one's analysis, might someday constitute malpractice; Brown agrees with that prospective direction. Neither identifies an existing malpractice requirement.
qs: Rather than it being unethical and risky to be using AI, are you actually doing your clients a disservice?
At some point, does it become malpractice not to use AI?

I think it does, because already I'm seeing that I'm just, across all my work, all my clients, I'm trying to do my best to persuade them of the benefits of AI and that it's safe, their data is safe, and it's a brave new world.

kp.k: Earlier deregulation enabled integrated patent and litigation practices
kp.d: As historical institutional context, Brown explains that UK patent attorneys and solicitors previously needed common qualifications to share a professional practice, sometimes requiring dual qualification. He says deregulation removed this constraint and enabled nonlawyer partners and more flexible structures. He places the change approximately 15 years earlier, possibly longer, and describes EIP's integration of patent attorneys and litigators as beneficial.
qs: up until probably 15 years ago now, maybe even longer, you couldn't have a mixed practice law firm.
You just had to all be solicitors or all be patent attorneys.
And so that was all deregulated and now you can have non-lawyer partners and it opens much more opportunity for effective law firm structures.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Brown claims that AI-native practice requires redesigned workflows and trained lawyers, and predicts that AI-native work could rapidly become the norm within EIP.
pts.d: Laurence Brown distinguishes AI-native practice from simply using ChatGPT, even effectively. His definition includes both minimally human firms and firms whose lawyers expect to work with AI and are trained accordingly. Visser AI is an AI-native legal service within EIP, not a software company; EIP still also operates traditionally. Based on uptake so far, he predicts an increasing share of AI-native work, potentially extending to all work surprisingly quickly, without setting a date.

pts.k: Brown claims hybrid human–AI services can deliver speed, quality and lower prices together, while supporting a shift toward fixed fees.
pts.d: Brown says clients increasingly demand demonstrable AI efficiencies, rather than superficial use. His own clients generally negotiate collaboratively over budgets and value rather than demanding billing only for dramatically reduced hours. He reports a standard client cost-reduction figure of about 30 percent and says fixed fees can benefit both clients and EIP without cutting attorneys out. Pricing still accounts for attorney time and unchanged overheads. These are claims about client pricing and service economics, not a quantified reduction in EIP's internal production costs.

pts.k: Brown claims AI improves patent preparation and enables parallel work, while human expertise remains necessary for claim drafting and verification.
pts.d: Brown describes AI helping attorneys probe inventions, generate additional inventor questions, extract technical details from meeting transcripts, structure drafts and improve readability. Senior attorneys can work on claims while juniors prepare the draft, replacing some sequential work with parallel activity. He expressly says AI remains poor at drafting high-quality patent claims. All output receives human checking, supplemented by AI critique in a fresh instance, sometimes using a different model. This describes augmentation, not direct reliance on autonomous output.

pts.k: Brown claims specialist patent tools outperform general-purpose AI for his patent work, and that workflow design contributes materially to their value.
pts.d: Brown reports substantial quality variation among specialist patent-AI providers and says the specialist platform Patently currently substantially outperforms Microsoft Copilot for the patent work he compares. He nevertheless finds general models effective for proofreading and summarisation. He attributes specialist advantages to context provision, interface features and workflow support, while acknowledging he is not an expert on Patently's underlying implementation. The comparison is task-specific rather than a claim that general models are inferior at every legal task.

pts.k: Brown suggests AI makes attorney work more enjoyable and that risk-centred regulation can discourage beneficial adoption.
pts.d: Brown personally finds AI's conversational mode more enjoyable, while explicitly allowing that this may reflect novelty. He does not claim it eliminates long working days. He argues European patent regulation has encouraged a conservative, risk-first approach, while recognising confidentiality risks as legitimate. He suggests the professional debate could already turn toward whether failing to use AI disadvantages clients. This is a normative suggestion, not a cited finding that non-use currently constitutes malpractice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Brown's direct practice experience, internal billing analysis and an internal comparison of six patent-AI providers.
pts.d: Brown grounds his commercial claims in client conversations, existing-client billing histories, fee proposals and reactions from prospective clients. He describes a test approximately 18 months before the interview in which six leading patent-AI providers received the same patent-specification drafting inputs and EIP partners rated and ranked their outputs. He also reports ongoing comparisons with Copilot and routine experience with AI-assisted preparation and drafting. The source supplies no test scores, sample sizes for commercial outcomes, measured turnaround reductions, or independent verification of the 30 percent pricing figure or maintained quality. His regulatory discussion includes an anecdote about another firm's usage-reporting form. Predictions of broad adoption and the emerging duty to use AI are extrapolations, not demonstrated future outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims describe current practice in the interview labelled 2026; broader adoption has no fixed deadline and benefits depend on workflow redesign, human oversight and confidentiality safeguards.
pts.d: EIP is explicitly still transitioning, and Brown's prediction that all work may become AI-native is qualified by 'maybe' and linked to uptake so far. His specialist-tool superiority claim is expressly current, not permanent. Quality must not decline for EIP's high-end clients, so human claim drafting and comprehensive verification remain central. Confidentiality arrangements, including no data retention and no training use, are described as essential to patent work. Fixed-fee savings must still cover lawyer time and overheads. His claim about enjoyment is qualified by possible novelty effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern premium patent services, corporate IP clients, volume filers and the attorneys delivering their work.
pts.d: Corporate clients and in-house patent lawyers face budget pressure and seek lower, predictable fees without reduced quality. Brown identifies volume patent filers as particularly strong beneficiaries because client familiarity and repeated work create economies of scale. Urgent filers benefit from faster preparation. Senior and junior patent attorneys retain substantive roles but work differently and more in parallel; Brown does not predict staffing cuts. EIP seeks to retain viable economics while reducing client prices. His regulatory concerns focus on European patent attorneys and the confidentiality of clients' inventions, not access-to-justice services or the whole legal market.
